'''James Grubbs Martin''' (born December 11, 1935) is an American chemist and politician who served as the [[List of governors of North Carolina|70th governor of North Carolina]] from 1985 to 1993. A member of the [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican Party]], he previously served six terms as the [[U.S. representative]] for [[North Carolina's 9th congressional district]] from 1973 to 1985.

Martin was the third Republican elected governor of North Carolina after [[Reconstruction era of the United States|Reconstruction]], the second since the [[1900 North Carolina gubernatorial election]], and the fifth overall. As of {{year}}, he was also the only Republican to serve two full terms as governor of the state. Since the passing of [[James Holshouser]] in 2013, Martin is North Carolina's oldest surviving governor. Since [[Jim Hunt]]'s death in 2025, Martin is also the last surviving governor to have served in the 20th century.

==Early life and education==
James Grubbs Martin was born on December 11, 1935, in [[Savannah, Georgia|Savannah]], and subsequently raised in [[South Carolina]]. He graduated from [[Davidson College]] in 1957 with a Bachelor of Science degree. Shortly after graduation, on June 1, he married [[Dottie Martin|Dorothy Ann McAulay]] of Charlotte, North Carolina.<ref name="Hunt papers 3">{{cite book|title=Addresses and Public Papers of James Baxter Hunt Jr. Governor of North Carolina Vol. III 1993–1997|year=2000|publisher=North Carolina Department of Cultural Resources|location=Raleigh, NC|isbn=0-86526-289-6|editor=Poff, Jan-Michael|pages=[https://archive.org/details/addressespublicp0000hunt/page/4 4–5]|url=https://archive.org/details/addressespublicp0000hunt/page/4}}</ref> An avid tuba player, he was a member of [[Phi Mu Alpha Sinfonia]] music fraternity and [[Beta Theta Pi]] Social Fraternity while an undergraduate at Davidson.{{citation needed|date=September 2012}}

==Academic career==
Martin received his PhD in chemistry from [[Princeton University]] in 1960, after completing a doctoral dissertation titled "Stereochemistry of the Diels-Alder reaction."<ref>{{Cite book|last=Martin|first=James G.|url=https://catalog.princeton.edu/catalog/2965647|title=Stereochemistry of the Diels-Alder reaction|date=1960|language=en}}</ref> He then served as an associate professor of [[chemistry]] at his alma mater Davidson College until 1972.<ref name="Hunt papers 3" /> As a professor at Davidson, he advised the school's Young Republicans chapter.

==Political career==
Martin registered as a member of the [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican Party]] in 1961 or 1962. He later explained, "I joined with the minority party because I felt the south needed two-party competition."{{sfn|Fleer|2007|p=77}} In 1966, he was elected to the [[Mecklenburg County, North Carolina|Mecklenburg County]] [[County commission|Board of Commissioners]]. He served for seven years, chairing the body from 1967 to 1968, and briefly in 1971. He was a president of the North Carolina Association of County Commissioners.

===House of Representatives (1973–1985)===
He was elected to the [[United States House of Representatives]] in 1972 representing the Charlotte-based [[North Carolina's 9th congressional district|9th Congressional district]].  He served there for six terms. He served as a [[United States House Committee on Ways and Means|Ways and Means Committee]] member, and as a House Republican Research Committee chairman. He became the first elected official to receive the [[Charles Lathrop Parsons Award]], given by the [[American Chemical Society]] for outstanding [[community service|public service]] by an American chemist, in 1983.<ref>{{cite web|title=Charles Lathrop Parsons Award|url=http://webapps.acs.org/findawards/detail.jsp?ContentId=CTP_004498|publisher=American Chemical Society|access-date=September 10, 2012|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304094244/http://webapps.acs.org/findawards/detail.jsp?ContentId=CTP_004498|archive-date=March 4, 2016}}</ref>

In 1984, with incumbent governor Jim Hunt leaving office due to the [[term limit]], Martin ran for the Republican nomination and won.  He defeated [[North Carolina Attorney General|state attorney general]] [[Rufus Edmisten]] by a nine-point margin.  He was helped by the coattails from [[Ronald Reagan]]'s landslide re-election victory.  He was also helped when [[Lieutenant Governor of North Carolina|Lieutenant Governor]] [[James C. Green|Jimmy Green]] endorsed him after being defeated by Edmisten in the Democratic primary.  Green was from eastern North Carolina, and his endorsement helped Martin win support among conservative Democrats in that part of the state.<ref>[http://www.carolinajournal.com/daily_journal/display.html?id=10552 Political grudges are nothing new] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150923200558/http://www.carolinajournal.com/daily_journal/display.html?id=10552 |date=September 23, 2015 }}, [[John Locke Foundation|Carolina Journal]] Online, John Hood, October 11, 2013. Retrieved April 17, 2014.</ref>

===Governor of North Carolina (1985–1993)===
{{BLP unreferenced section|date=March 2019}}
While most political figures running for office were prone to make promises covering a wide range of issues from education to health care, Martin made one promise that garnered a lot of attention; he said he would address all of the priorities in the state, but his only promise was that construction on [[Interstate 40 in North Carolina|Interstate 40]] from Raleigh to [[Wilmington, North Carolina]] would be finished before he left office. The long-neglected and last leg of I-40 from [[Barstow, California]] would open up the southeastern coastal area to the rest of the state.  He was true to his promise; the last unfinished leg of I-40 was finished before the end of his first term.

{{Further|1988 North Carolina gubernatorial election}}
Martin was easily reelected in 1988, defeating Lieutenant Governor [[Robert B. Jordan, III|Bob Jordan]] by 13 points. In so doing, he became the only member of his party to have been elected to two terms as governor of North Carolina. He was part of a 28-year trend of Governors of North Carolina who were named James, having been preceded and succeeded by [[Jim Hunt]], who in turn was preceded in his first term by [[James Holshouser]].

==Later life==
In 1993, Martin retired from political life and became chairman of the board of the James Cannon Research Center of [[Carolinas Medical Center]] in Charlotte, North Carolina. In 2012, he was appointed to lead an investigation into academic improprieties at the [[University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill]].<ref>[http://www.wral.com/news/education/story/11436603/ WRAL: Former governor to dig deeper into UNC academics]</ref> For the [[2016 United States presidential election|United States presidential election in 2016]], Martin endorsed fellow Republican [[John Kasich presidential campaign, 2016|John Kasich]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.newsobserver.com/news/politics-government/politics-columns-blogs/under-the-dome/article65943932.html|title=NC's presidential endorsement list|work=NewsObserver}}</ref>

== Works ==
* ''Revelation through Science'' (2016)

==Legacy==
In January 2017, the Pope Center for Higher Education Policy changed its name to the [[James G. Martin Center for Academic Renewal]], named after Governor Martin.<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www.jamesgmartin.center/2017/01/new-era-james-g-martin-center-academic-renewal/|title=A New Era: The James G. Martin Center for Academic Renewal — The James G. Martin Center for Academic Renewal|date=January 3, 2017|newspaper=The James G. Martin Center for Academic Renewal|language=en-US|access-date=January 3, 2017}}</ref> Gov. Martin also serves on the board of directors for the Martin Center.<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www.jamesgmartin.center/about/board-of-directors/|title=Board of Directors — The James G. Martin Center for Academic Renewal|newspaper=The James G. Martin Center for Academic Renewal|language=en-US|access-date=January 3, 2017}}</ref> The Eastern Half of the [[Interstate 485|Charlotte Outerbelt]] is named the James G. Martin Freeway.
